steps.label: Bit Shifts and Two's Complement
steps.content:
Number Systems

Bit Shifts and Two's Complement

Year 10, 1.1 L4

steps.label: Logical Shift Left
steps.content:
Logical Shift Left

  • A logical shift moves every bit the same number of places in the same direction.
  • Shifting left moves bits toward the 128 column.
  • Any bit pushed off the left end is lost completely.
  • Every column emptied on the right is filled with a 0.

steps.label: Practice: Shift Left

Practice: Shift Left

Four questions to check you have got it, then unlimited extension practice for anyone who finishes early.

steps.label: Logical Shift Right
steps.content:
Logical Shift Right

  • Shifting right moves bits toward the 1s column.
  • Any bit pushed off the right end is lost completely.
  • Every column emptied on the left is filled with a 0.
  • The number of places to shift is always given in the question.

steps.label: Check Your Understanding
steps.content:
Check Your Understanding

Questions to ask around the room:

  • What happens to a bit that gets pushed off the end of the register during a shift?
  • What value goes into a column left empty by a shift?
  • Which direction moves bits toward the 128 column?
  • If you shift 00000011 left by 3 places, what is the result?
  • Why might a shift lose information that a normal conversion never would?

steps.label: Two's Complement: Storing Negative Numbers
steps.content:
Two's Complement: Storing Negative Numbers

  • Positive numbers in two's complement are written exactly like ordinary binary, with a leading 0.
  • To store a negative number, first write its positive value in 8-bit binary.
  • Invert every bit: flip each 1 to 0 and each 0 to 1.
  • Add 1 to the inverted result. That is the two's complement value.

steps.label: Two's Complement: Back to Denary
steps.content:
Two's Complement: Back to Denary

  • The leftmost bit is worth -128 instead of +128. Every other column keeps its usual positive value.
  • Add up the value of every column containing a 1, including the -128 column if it is set.
  • If the leftmost bit is 0, the total is positive and works exactly like ordinary binary.
  • If the leftmost bit is 1, the total is always negative.

steps.label: Check Your Understanding
steps.content:
Check Your Understanding

Questions to ask around the room:

  • What is different about the leftmost bit in two's complement, compared to ordinary binary?
  • What are the three steps for converting a negative denary number into two's complement?
  • What sign does a number have if its leftmost bit is 1?
  • What is the smallest and largest value an 8-bit two's complement register can store?
  • How would you write positive 50 in 8-bit two's complement, without doing any of the invert-and-add-1 steps?
